utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we begin, there are one or two housekeeping matters. First of all, the registrar has an announcement about yesterday's exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Exhibit -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 326 tab 9, which was tendered through Witness C-1220 is marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So that that's understood, it's marked for identification only and will have to be produced by another witness. I'm going to deal with one other matter before we continue with the cross-examination. Ms. Higgins, we have seen correspondence involving your position here and that Mr. Kay will not be here for some weeks because of other matters. We take the view and our decision is this: That you may be in court as an assistant to the amicus for the six weeks involved. You may address the Trial Chamber where appropriate, and of course you should be remunerated appropriately, and we will have that sent to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now for you to continue your cross-examination of this witness. You covered a great deal of ground yesterday. We approve of that because you did it fairly quickly. So we think that you probably could finish within half an hour, but if there is more time that you want, then of course it's open to you to ask for it at the end and we'll consider the position. But we hope you could finish within half an hour with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I asked you whether you knew that before these events that you describe at the beginning of your statement, dozens of military facilities and barracks of the JNA in Croatia were blocked. Do you know about these attacks and I'm talking about the period up to the 12th of November, 1991, that tens of members of the JNA had lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I know that barracks had been blocked, but I cannot say anything about casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, is it correct that about a week before the JNA launched its military action in Saborsko, the one that you were talking about, that is to say on the 6th or 7th approximately, November, that is, 1991, members of the ZNG in Saborsko, above Licka Jesenica, that's one kilometre away from Saborsko, they killed in an atrocious manner three Serbs: Susnjar, Stevan; Susnjar, Milan, nicknamed Mijat, and they cut off his fingers; and Petrovic, Bogdan. They cut off his ears and stabbed him with a knife 100 times all over his body while he was still alive. Do you remember the killing of these three men and this event?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the event and I know that they were killed in a cruel way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that members of this broken up ZNG, after Saborsko was abandoned upon this action that you described on the 15th of November in the village of Dabar, they took prisoner 15 Serbs, and they took them to Josipdol and then killed them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Except that I don't know the actual number, but I think that it involves 15 persons. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that the youngest of them was 16 years old? His name was Bude Cveticanin, Mile Parenta was killed, Mile Lolic as well and several members of the Klis family. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that their bodies were never handed over to the families? The members of the ZNG burned them, and in the spring of 1992, they handed over their urns to the command of the Lika Corps in Korenica. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the paramilitary forces incessantly over the days that preceded this information that you -- this operation that you are talking about in terms of deblocking Saborsko, attacked the military barracks and the military facility that is above Licka Jesenica and that is only about one kilometre away from Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the army set out to deblock the attack military facility which was one of the greatest depots of fuel for the army in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that members of the paramilitaries attacked the military facility, the training ground in Slunj that was of military and strategic significance because this is where the command post of the 5th Army was of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, if I understood you correctly, that the air force started this attack on Saborsko. Did you see the air force attack Saborsko, bomb Saborsko, shoot?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, missiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this statement that you gave to the MUP in Karlovac and which is attached to your statement, you say two or three times Saborsko was flown over by two Mig 21s.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you did not say that they bombed them. You say that they flew over.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, maybe I thought that they flew over a few times, and they also shot missiles. That's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Flew over. Precisely in this statement that you gave to the police, on the 8th of November, 1999, you did not mention anywhere that the aircraft bombed Saborsko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think -- well, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, that's what you meant. All right. Is it correct that members of the ZNG shot one aeroplane and took the pilot prisoner? His name was Janjic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: You mean over there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know about this area. I don't know. I don't know, but maybe perhaps in the area beyond maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us just deal with a brief matter. You said yesterday that arms were distributed. I wrote down here that you said that on the boxes it said M-4. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Among the other signs, I meant that that's what it said too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the army, among its weapons, for several decades before that did not have any more M-48 rifles?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: In this area there were semi-automatic rifles and M-48s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I assume that this comes from some of the TO reserves, because the regular troops did not have those rifles for a long time. Was this from some depot that was in your area? You mentioned a depot, actually, one that you had in your own area?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, possibly. I cannot tell. I mean, I don't know where this came from. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this depot, this military depot, the one that you said was near your town?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: It was in the centre of town itself. This is where the barracks were and also the depot within the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it was my understanding that you got rid of the map. So I'm not going to ask him anything about the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He couldn't identify it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you do not know who the commander of the brigade was subordinated to, but you assumed that the command was in Korenica or Plitvice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know that I was asked that question. The command of the division was in Korenica, rather in the village of Mukinje, Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you don't know who the commander was?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Suput. I've just remembered a name. Suput. When he was there, at what time, I don't know, but any rate, I know that his name was mentioned, that is that he was commander of the division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, you mentioned that the TO afterwards got artillery weapons as well. What kind of artillery weapons did they get from the TO? You only mentioned mortars, but these are infantry weapons. Any company has that. Did they get any kind of artillery, the TO?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Mortars, 120 millimetres, 82 millimetres, and also anti-aircraft guns, yes. Now, what kind of weapons these are, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As for training, you explained that there were reservists there or, rather, soldiers who were doing their military service, and of course they were trained to use such weapons.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were those who served in all the arms and services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked where these supplies came from and you said that you did not know. You just know that there was a big depot there nearby. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Tell me one more thing: Is it correct that somebody forcibly mobilised you in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: With call-up papers. I was supposed to report at my wartime unit at such-and-such a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you think that somebody forced you to report to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I had to. Everybody had to. Everybody up to the age of 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you think that that was your duty?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm just interested in a few things in respect of what you were talking about a yesterday. First of all, out of those 32 men who remained jobless that day, as you had put it, when the situation calmed down, did anybody go back to work?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 32 men, are they in that area now at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are they?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: There are a few of them in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of the 4.000 people from that area that lived there in your area, how many of them are there now?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't think that even 30 per cent are left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about all of Ogulin, including the surrounding area, this area in general, this area of yours? How many people have remained?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, approximately.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: At that place, I don't think that there are more than 200 people left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. You said when what happened happened on the 12th of November that you all returned to Saborsko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First you returned when what happened on the 12th of November happened.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you returned to Saborsko; right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, nobody stayed in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to ask you. So from Saborsko you all returned to your homes?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed at home?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened happened, and you all went home and then you did not go any more.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: We only held the position, guarded the positions. I don't know how to put this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you all at your homes?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes. But we went there every day in shifts. It depended on the shift you had. So then we went to these positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a few matters, and for the first matter I would like to request a private session because I want to clarify a matter related to the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during your testimony in the beginning, you spoke about the training facility near Slunj. You spoke about the military posts in Mukinje and others facilities in your region. During the cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic asked you whether the training facility, et cetera, was under blockade, and your answer to this was, "Well, they were in that area." And now I would want to clarify. Was the training facility in Slunj under blockade in November 1991, at the time of the attack on Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in Slunj. Korenica, no. In Mukinje, they had a link to Knin. The war in Bosnia had not broken out yet, so you could communicate even with Yugoslavia then. But this training facility, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- who -- does that mean they couldn't leave the training facility any more? Was it blocked in front? Was the blockade in front of it? Can you explain that, what you mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I can, but then I don't know whether you can understand what I'm saying. You probably don't know this well enough, so it's hard for me to explain this situation to you. Plaski is here, Slunj is over there, and up here is Saborsko and over here an Ogulin. And this area around here, that's where the training facility was between Plaski and Slunj. And now it was also under blockade just like the entire town of Plaski. Whereas Mukinje, that's where the command was, I said that, the command of the division was in Mukinje, and that is on the other side of the Plitvice lakes. So this is no longer -- I mean, this is behind Saborsko. This is behind Plitvice. It's towards Korenica. Mukinje, Korenica, that's only 4 or 5 kilometres, I mean away from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I would like to know is: Was there a blockade, a roadblock or anything blocking the training facility? Couldn't they move out at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Only on the assumption that they were stronger and that they could get out by force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic referred, during the cross-examination to Saborsko as a Croatian stronghold that needed to be eliminated to deblockade the road. And now I would like to know, was it necessary to eliminate Saborsko to deblockade the road?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: That is the only direction leading out of Plaski then, leading out of this encirclement, except for those forest paths that I refer to, one forest path that goes through the forest only. Nobody could ensure safe passage along that path.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it necessary to totally destroy Saborsko to get through?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, had they been smart, they shouldn't have destroyed Saborsko at least. That's how I see it. But they couldn't reach an agreement. All I'm saying -- I'm saying only what I know. It is rumoured that they had offered to allow the passage through in exchange for not destroying the place. And why that didn't occur, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had offered to allow the passage through?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: This was said by the then-authorities in the municipality. And allegedly the authorities in the place, in the town, offered that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is what you call -- it was -- you didn't hear that. You said this was rumoured.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I said that I didn't participate in the political life there, and I wasn't involved. This was a rumour going around that there was an offer like this and that the people from Saborsko did not accept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it necessary to transport the old people, the old Croat people from Saborsko out of the region to deblockade the road and make it safe?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: When Saborsko was taken, the elderly that remained there, and there were mostly elderly that remained there, they were taken to Licka Jesenica. They spent the night there. And the following day they were taken in buses, in two buses towards Ogulin, the line that I mentioned before, and this was how they were allowed to go to the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of the presence of policemen during the attack, you said during the examination-in-chief that you saw policemen in Saborsko after the attack. You said they would all come down into the centre. Mr. Milosevic asked you whether the police was there, and you said that you did not see the police because you were on one side and they were on the other side. Your answer, does this refer to the attack as such or what does it refer to, your answer that you were on one side and they on the other?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: During -- during that operation, I wanted to say this to you but I probably wasn't successful. While the attack was going on, we had no connection. There was no connection between my group and the police. We could not establish a connection. We couldn't see each other then. And then later on when everything was over, all of us were leaving in groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the testimony in chief, you described that two or three people you saw looting, and you said that they belonged to the Martic police. And you also referred to the killing of Krtan. Mr. Milosevic referred to this killing of Krtan as well, and he read to you part of your previous statement to the MUP Croatia. In the part he read to you, you refer to a certain page, and those who were with him who did it, the killing of Krtan. Those who killed Krtan, were they soldiers, police, or civilians?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Members of police, Martic's police. They were members of that police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those Martic policemen who killed Krtan, and you mentioned this Pejic, are these the same people that you saw looting in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the part that was read to you, you said that it was Pejic and those who were with him. Who are the others? Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The name of Lecin, Cvekic and Pejic was mentioned and they are sort of brothers. All I know is that it involves several people, several people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the MUP Croatia in 1999, you saw mentioned being involved a certain Snjaka. Snjaka, that's a nickname. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Snjaka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose nickname is that? Snjaka, who is that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Djuro Ogrizovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have to clarify this question, because I understood the witness to say yesterday when I questioned him, I understood that he said that Krtan was killed by two or three men who were looters, robbers. And then I asked him, "Why didn't you report this to police?" And he answered saying that nobody was able to report this to police because they were armed. That's how I understood him yesterday. And now he's saying that they were members of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to bring this to an end. Now, then, who is it who killed Krtan? We're not going on about this. Can you help us, Witness C-1220? Who is it who killed Krtan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody misunderstood here me or perhaps I was unable to express things the way I should have. In the positions where we were - I don't want to go into this again - but let me just say this that the first information -- that was the first time we learned that there were dead people there. Bogdan Pesut-Cubra came and he was in tears. And he told us then they killed Pero Krtan and somebody else. And that was the first time we heard of it, and he was crying then. And then he said Peic, Lecin and Cvekic were there in that group who had killed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who were those three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were members of Martic's Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what Mr. Milosevic inquired about is this: What I wanted to say was that those people were the kind of people who had no trouble reaching for arms. They were thugs. They were able to kill anyone. They simply didn't care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. We cannot continue this. Now, the witness has given his answer and his clarification. Witness C-1220, thank you very much for come to the court to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While arrangements are being made for the witness to go, may I raise just a couple of administrative matters, to use the time? Mr. Groome will be taking the next witness and he has a mater to raise as well. None of this will take very long. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. First, there is an application with Registry for variation of protective measures in respect of an upcoming witness. I know it takes some time for applications to find their way to Chambers. We have copies available for your consideration, and we'll make those available now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I must say, speaking for myself, I'm concerned about the number of applications in this case, this part of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Protective measures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm concerned that there are so many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry that you should be concerned, but I'm afraid that the position is absolutely straightforward and is as follows: If people come here and we discover that they have sought or we have sought on their behalf more protective measures than on careful analysis that they require, we regularly reduce the level of protection we require. On the other hand, where people face threats and are aware at a later stage of proceedings that they are at far greater risk than they previously appreciated, it is absolutely our responsibility to make application on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be but it is also our duty to have a trial that is held in public and open to the public as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say that we are doing everything we can to ensure that, and the criticism of the Prosecution that Your Honour is, by implication, making is one I have to reject. There are great risks associated with giving evidence in this court. There are risks that have been aggravated recently by what's been happening in the press, and you will see from this particular document that they are risks that are serious on individuals. We take those matters extremely seriously. We have a very high duty to these witnesses, and we are not bringing applications on, say, where it is unnecessary but as you will discover in respect of the next witness, wherever we can make previously protected witnesses -- not make, whenever we are in a position to call witnesses publicly who would otherwise be subject to some measure of protection, we do so. I would press Your Honours to consider this application in due course, not of course immediately, as one that is worthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me raise something else about this witness I notice. He doesn't appear to be on your list provided on the 31st of July. I don't see his name. Described as witness planning until the 1st of January. Unless I'm mistaken about that, I don't find his name. No need to look for it now. I just want to be sure that we're not getting more witnesses in than we originally had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness sit down while we're dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with -- can I come back to that later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I press the general point on the Chamber and ask the Chamber really to consider our record of witnesses who come here and have given evidence publicly where previously there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only point I make is there seems to be a difference in -- to the parts of the case. Now, there may be a good reason for that, but it's one which is very noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to that, it may well be that A, there is a difference in the character of the type of witness generally we're calling in this part of the segment of the case from what happened in the other part of the case. It may well be that because of the different circumstances, the risks are profoundly different. The former Yugoslavia is a dangerous place, and those of us who have to go there and deal with it are well aware of that and take these things extremely seriously. Your Honour, can I turn to something different? Two other points. First, there is another meeting organised tomorrow at 4.00 being run by Mr. Saxon, but I'll be present, in respect of Rule 68. As you know we provide reports on a regular basis and we have meetings on a regular basis where the amici are invited and I'm happy to say that both Ms. Higgins and Mr. Tapuskovic are going to turn up tomorrow. Previously Mr. Wladimiroff has attended. The associates of the accused have been invited. They have not indicated an intention to attend. I repeat publicly through the court that invitation. If they don't turn up and contribute to the Rule 68 discussions, then any concerns that the accused may have about Rule 68 disclosures are matters that we simply cannot respond to. The presence of his associates at this sort of meeting which we've offered would help us deal with other matters, and I just give one example. There are some indications from the accused of witnesses he now intends to call. His language has to be listened to quite carefully. I might want, where it appears to me that there is a witness to be called by the accused, to take particular precautions before speaking to such witnesses myself if I'd already formed the view that I was going to speak to them. Without contact with the associates, that sort of useful dialogue is impossible. And the third point that I wanted to raise at some stage and I raise now is this, it comes in two parts: We have in mind and have had in mind for some weeks now that it might be helpful for the Chamber to have CD-ROMs containing material sorted by witness in a way that would be electronically searchable for those who prefer to work electronically, and we're in some way advanced in relation to this as an exercise. But in light of recent problems with newspapers, we are putting a temporary hold on it while we review the position, mindful of the fact that a CD-ROM misused would provide a very great deal of information, not all of it information that would necessarily have been given in public, improperly to people who might have an interest in having it. It's simply too easy to abuse. So we're giving thought to it and we'll come back to you on that. But with that in mind, we have one particular matter we'd like just to mention without one minute expecting the Chamber to give a view on it today, but if we can just ask you to think about it. The summaries we provide for assistance of the Court, and we believe them to be extremely useful as a tool, of course not exhibited and we don't ask them to be exhibited, but they don't form part of the record in any sense. Query whether they should just for purposes of having a complete record be in some way part of the record, as it were, supplements to the other 65 ter summaries, something of that sort. If the Court could at some stage give thought to it. It's not a high priority. We can, of course, take appropriate steps to ensure that they would be, if they were to become part of the record, submitted in some recordable form. And I mention it at the same time as dealing with the CD-ROM possibility, because if we are in due course either part way through the trial or at the end of it to provide for assistance CD-ROMs to presumably all parties that contain a lot of the material that's already been given, then one of the items that might go on that as well as the 65 ter summary would be the court summary. But not for -- it's just a matter for consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We would have to think about that because I'm not sure what form that could take. If they're the exhibits, it seems to me they don't form part of the record. But of course we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter which while we're on these is not to forget the paper summaries that you were making, and I have in mind the document that you were providing about Kosovo to all parties of your summary, as it were, of your case, and I think it needs updating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could see to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the fill-box document, as it were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've forgotten what its term was. Yes, I think it's that, but it was your summary at the end which you offered to all, and we certainly got an edition it have, but it needs completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's obviously a regular work in progress and we will be delighted to make it available periodically and I'll draw that to the attend of the people concerned. Mr. Groome has the next witness and a point to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a few minutes ago I received an e-mail message regarding this witness. Witness C-004 is the subject of some protective measures and I received an e-mail from the investigator stating that this witness is now asking that the protective measures be withdrawn and that he testify openly. Before the Court rules on it, I would like to bring the Court aware of the brief history of protective measures regarding this witness. This past Friday, this witness informed me that it was his wish to proceed in open session. Friday afternoon I intended to bring that to the Court's attention on Monday. Friday afternoon the Office of the Prosecutor received information from a government that they had just received information regarding a threat against this witness, and I can provide more details about that in private session should the Chamber wish. We immediately informed this witness of that threat and the application on Monday was then not undertaken. As Judge Hunt has pointed out in other cases before this Tribunal, while the wish of the witness carries some significant weight, it not necessarily dispositive of a determination that the Chamber may make regarding protective measures which are necessary. I would ask that if this witness -- if we can verify that this is the intention of this witness to proceed in open session by simply asking him that question here, it would be the Prosecution's position that that application be withdrawn and that he be permitted to testify in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Perhaps you would like to ascertain the witness's views before we go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask, Witness C-004 -- Witness C-004, I would ask you at this stage, is it your decision to proceed with your testimony in open session and not have any of the protective measures that have been afforded you by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And have you given this careful consideration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is satisfied and would move to withdraw our previous application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The witness can give evidence in open, session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just -- in a related matter, Your Honour, the witness in his statement mentioned the name of somebody who he expressed some concern that if that person were to be discussed in open court, that person may be jeopardised. I would ask and he has asked me to convey when we mention the name if we can go into private session, he's asking that Mr. Milosevic, if he wants to inquire about this person, to do so in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Milosevic hears that and we can go into private session to discuss that particular person. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection based on principle. The opposite side for the umpteenth time is bringing in witnesses here as secret witnesses and like a magician takes the curtain off and proclaims them to be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not a proper objection, as you know quite well. You know who those witnesses are. The Tribunal -- just a moment. The Tribunal has a power to protect its witnesses whether they're Prosecution or Defence witnesses, and it is a power which it will use. You have heard me express my view about it, that on the whole proceedings should be open, but there are occasions where it is necessary that witnesses should be protected. Now, this witness has clearly thought very carefully about the matter and has come to the conclusion that he will give evidence in open session. There is no question of trickery or anything of that sort on the part of the Prosecution who have behaved perfectly properly in the way they brought this matter before us. Now, let us continue with the witness's evidence. No, Mr. Milosevic. It's not a matter for argument. Now, let us continue with the witness's evidence. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Groome Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Jovan Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us for what publication you worked in the years 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Politika Ekspres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what publication do you currently work for?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: A weekly, Vreme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Chamber what particular areas of focus your reporting has concerned itself with during your profession?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I have worked in the -- the department which followed the judiciary, courts, prosecutor's office, police, and crime-related events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the general area of Serbia in which you were born?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the spring of 1991. Did you have occasion to travel around Eastern Slavonia in connection with your duties as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And continuing throughout the summer of 1991, the fall and throughout 1992, did you also have occasion to travel into the Vukovar area as well as other areas of Croatia and Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to briefly describe the process that you follow when you write a story?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I try to talk as much as possible with people, and I try to make my own observations, and this is what I enter into my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you then submit whatever story you write to the editors at your publication?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes from the field via the telephone I dictate it to those who make notes in my editor's office, and sometimes if it's not too far, I go back to Belgrade, turn in my story and then return back to the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to travelling to the Vukovar area, were you required to obtain permission from the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: In the very beginning, my journalist's ID was sufficient. And later on, a permit was required to work there issued by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive permission to travel to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender a binder containing 13 exhibits which I intend to use with this exhibit. It contains documents, photographs, and transcripts of video recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, let me raise one particular matter in relation to this practice which we in fact find a useful one, speaking for the Trial Chamber, to have these documents tendered to us in binder form and before the witness gives evidence. But the problem which arises is this, and it arose with the last witness: That it may be that the documents are eventually not exhibited, which requires then the housekeeping matter of returning documents, particularly with an accused who isn't represented. So what we need to do is this: That we will -- the practice, as I say, we find a very useful one and therefore we will continue with, but what we must be careful to do is at the end of a witness's evidence, we ensure that all the documents which are in a binder or in a clip have in fact been exhibited, and in that way we will keep the housekeeping straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I'd ask you to take a look at the document contained in tab 1. I would ask you, is that the permission form that you received authorising you to travel to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us who issued that authorisation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Secretariat for National Defence did, or, rather, the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you applied for and received authorisation to travel into Bosnia, more specifically the area of Visegrad in connection with your duties as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown the document in tab 2 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go any further, we ought to give the binder a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 342.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, looking at Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 2, is that the permission or authorisation you received to travel into Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide the originals of both of those documents to the officer of the -- the Office of the Prosecutor here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of your work, were you required to apply for authorisations to travel to other areas of Bosnia as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you questions regarding the events that you personally witnessed, I want to ask you to give a brief description of the people who you will be testifying about, and I will begin with those people who were members of the Yugoslav army. Do you know or did you know a person by the name of Colonel Enes Taso?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who he is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Pancevo Mechanised Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- do you know a Major Veselin Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is he?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Guards Brigade that was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Captain Aleksandar Bojkovski?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Bojkovski, captain of the Yugoslav army, and he was also in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you do you know a person by the name of Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now ask that the witness be shown a photograph that is marked as Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 3. Then I would ask that that be placed on the overhead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, do you recognise the person depicted in Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 3?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who do you recognise that to be?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: That is Captain Miroslav Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Spasoje Petkovic, also known as Stuka?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for us who that person?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He was a regular soldier in the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now want to ask you about members of the Territorial Defence. Do you know a person by the name of Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who he is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 1st Detachment of the Territorial Defence in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look to your left on the overhead projector and look at what is Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 4. Do you recognise the man that is depicted in that picture?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who do you recognise him to be?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: That is Stanko Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ivica Andric?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who he was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: A volunteer who was also in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he work with Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was there with Stanko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you about a person by the name of Radovan Stojicevic, also known as Badza. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he associated with one of the Territorial Defence units in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He was with the unit that was in Erdut, and he was in the leadership of the Republican MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Republican MUP," which republic are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last person associated with Territorial Defence units I want to ask you about is a person by the name of Marko Pavlovic. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a description or tell us how you know him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know him as the commander of the Territorial Defence in -- in Visegrad or -- just a moment, please. No, in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that Zvornik in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zvornik is in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime after you first knew him, did you come to learn that he had a different name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you learn his other name to be?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Quite a long time afterwards I learnt this and talked to him, and I knew him as Branko Popovic. It was, in fact, Branko Popovic. That's who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also come to learn whether or not he had an association with the person by the name of Mihalj Kertes?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That he -- how shall I put it? He was Mihalj Kertes's man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about members of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you know a person or did you know a person by the name of Momir Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him in Vukovar or, rather, in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you saw him in Erdut, did you hear other officers and other soldiers refer to him by some other name other than Momir Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would address him as Colonel Peric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that the Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 5, be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dulovic, I'd ask you to take a look at that exhibit. Do you recognise the person who is in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That is Momir Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that fairly represent how he appeared in Erdut when you saw him when he was referred to as Colonel Peric?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Momir Gavrilovic alive today?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when he died?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He was killed on the 3rd of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: That killing remained unsolved, but he was killed by a firearm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After his death, did the police, did the Republic of Serbian MUP publish the details about his true identity and his curriculum, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. positions he held?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in its entirety. But there was just one period missing where he was and what he did from 1991 until, let's say, 1995 or 1993. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the positions that were published prior to 1991 and after 1995, were they all positions within the Serbian Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Positions in the state security of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask that you now look at Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 6, and ask you do you recognise that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Momir Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the picture of Mr. Gavrilovic that was published at the time of his murder in August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some members of paramilitary groups. Do you know a person by the name of Zeljko Raznjatovic, also known as Arkan?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you ever seen him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it that you saw him in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: 1991. In the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Borovo Selo in the vicinity of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a suburb of Vukovar, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did men associated with Arkan, did they have any unique piece of uniform that they wore?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have a unique uniform that they wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was -- what was unique about that uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: They were unique because his men wore black woolen Balaclavas, and when you place them over your face, they had slits for the eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the course of your duties as a journalist that you had -- you were shown a document purporting to be a loan from the Serbian state security to Zeljko Raznjatovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the circumstances under which you were shown this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: This happened at the trial of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, who was accused of grievous bodily harm, that is to say breaking a civilian's arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who showed you that document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: His lawyers who asked that the trial be held in closed session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the amount of money that was loaned to Arkan by the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the Serbian MUP, it was the Federal MUP and it was a credit, a loan. The Federal SUP gave him a loan, but I don't remember the sum of money involved. I did see the figure. I think it was around 10 million dinars at that time, his repayment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For those of us who are not familiar with the dinar, could you approximate what that would be in Deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date of this loan?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Major Peja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'd like the witness to say a little more about the loan. What was it on the document that specifically indicated that it was a loan? Was there a repayment programme?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, you've heard Judge Robinson's question. Did you see anything on the document that indicated to you a repayment schedule?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: From the document that I glanced at briefly, all that could be seen was that a loan was granted by the Federal SUP, that it had granted a loan to Arkan, and it mentioned the figure to be repaid every month from his salary or whatever. I saw the stamp and seal of the Federal SUP and the heading where it said "The Federal SUP." And it was a document that proves that the loan was granted him by the Federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The interpreter misspoke. It was 9 million.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just saw this for one brief moment. His lawyers asked that the trial be closed to the public. However, the Trial Chamber did not accept that and the trial went public. At the time, what I wanted to see was whether it was true, whether the Federal SUP did in fact give him the loan. And the Federal SUP gives loans only to its own members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you might let us know later what 9 million dinars would be in Deutschmarks and also in perhaps dollars and euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the word "salary" in the last answer you gave. Did it indicate Arkan's place of employment on this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on the basis of the existence of this document that the attorney for Arkan was seeking to have the proceedings in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you about Major Peja. Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of -- he was one of the officers of Zeljko Raznjatovic "Arkan."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see him present in the Vukovar area in the summer and fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another member of Arkan's group by the name of Peja?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have another name that he was known by to distinguish him from Major Peja?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They called him Peja Ciganin or Peja the Gypsy in translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Vojislav Seselj?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you briefly describe for us who he is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He is the president of the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 7, and that it be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I'd ask you do you recognise the who is depicted in that photograph, the person in the centre of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: That is Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Miroslav, and the nickname, or he's also known as Cele?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who do you know him to be?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of a group of Seselj's men as they were called. An armed unit, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person who was known as Kameni?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him. I know him from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he associated with any particular group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Also associated with Seselj's men in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know a person by the name of Mica Teodosijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is he or was he associated with a particular group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Mica Teodosijevic was also one of Seselj's men, one of the vojvodas or dukes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have another name that you heard him referred to or referred as?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was his nickname, Mica Srafciger. Srafciger was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the translators to translate that word in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Screwdriver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 10 -- I'm sorry, tab 9, and I would note for the Chamber, tab 9 is a marked-up version of tab 8 which is a blank copy of the same photograph should it be necessary to show it to other witnesses. Do you recognise some of the people in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is handwriting on this photograph. Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the pointer, I would ask you to indicate the person you know as Cele.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person you know as Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person you know as "the Screwdriver."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with a paramilitary organisation by the name of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the leader of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Vojin Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what areas of the former Yugoslavia do you know him from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I know Cele from Zvornik or, rather, I met him in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript has indicated you said Cele. I'm asking you now about Vojin Vuckovic. Can you tell us where you know him from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vojin Vuckovic is a man I met, and he drew my attention during a trial held in Belgrade, a trial of the brothers Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Vojin Vuckovic on trial for?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: The Vuckovic brothers, Vojin and Dusan were their names, Arkan [As interpreted] Repic, that was his brother, they were on trial, and it was the first trial. They were on trial for war crimes or, rather, Repic Dusan was charged of war crimes. Vojin was accused of some minor criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of that trial did Vojin Vuckovic testify about any relationship he had with an official body of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite get your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of that trial, did he testify regarding any relationship or -- that he may have had with an organisation or institution of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vojin Vuckovic was the commander of the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention any relationship or testify about any relationship with an official organ of the government?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was an instructor for the martial arts in the Federal SUP as he himself told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're just slightly past the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you remember in this and any other adjournment there may be about this case not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that also includes the members of the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue, just in response to Judge Robinson's inquiry about the currency, all we've been able to find over the break is current valuations. I will attempt to get an earlier valuation so that the Chamber has some range. But I also want to note that the interpreters have corrected that the witness did not say 10 million but instead said 9 million. So the conversion of 9 million Yugoslav dinars equals 146.570 US dollars or 149.322 euros, or 292.048 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, before I continue, I would like to just ask you a couple of questions about your testimony before the break. The trial of Arkan, can you tell us approximately when that trial was held?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: In the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the trial of the Vuckovic brothers that you referred to, when was that held?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with a paramilitary group known as Dusan Silni? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I don't know of any other details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever personally see members of that group in your work in either Vukovar or Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I did see them, but I did not have an opportunity of identifying them. I don't think so really. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to ask you about two individuals and ask you to tell us something about them. A woman by the name of Dragica.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I first saw Dragica in Vukovar within a Territorial Defence unit, one that was led by Stanko Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us her approximate age at that time and where she was from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: She said to me that she was 30 something, 32 or 33, and she was from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's Novi Sad in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she also known by another name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your work in the Vukovar area in the summer and fall of 1991, did you come to see a man whose trial you covered in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not see him in Vukovar or did you not cover the trial?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, I did cover his trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see him sometime later in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, not Vukovar. Later. Later when his trial took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him outside after courtroom and in possession of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the concept of Vojna Linija?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that concept, but I did not have any reliable information about the details involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that you did have before you describe it to us, would you tell us what the basis of the information you do possess regarding it? What is the basis of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about it from people who I assume knew about that. So I heard about that from conversations with certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you assume that these people knew about it by virtue of the position that they held?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the position or positions that were held by the people who informed you of this Vojna Linija?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: In the top echelons of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us briefly what is the concept of Vojna Linija?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the police there was a certain number of people who would complete the military academy, the land forces academy, and then they would return to the police with the knowledge that they acquired there. That's what I had been told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the concept or this thing we're calling the Vojna Linija, do you know whether it was established prior to the conflict, during the conflict, or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Even before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your work, have you ever been able to interview anybody you believed to be a member of this group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: This was not an official, on-the-record interview. It was background discussion with these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the people you had this discussion with identify themselves or admit to you that they were a member of the Vojna Linija?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was a fluid organisation, so to speak, to the best of my knowledge, and it was never made public or was any information about it published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to some events that you personally witnessed, and I'd like to begin by drawing your attention to the summer and fall of 1991, and I would ask you, were you travelling in Croatia, in particular in the vicinity of Vukovar, in the course of your duties as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time during that period of time when you saw the build-up of troops in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, around Vukovar. On both sides, for that matter. Both sides of Vukovar, that is. The side where Borovo Selo is and the side where Negoslavci is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you said build-up by both sides, do you mean both sides of Vukovar geographically or both sides to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Geographically. I mean on both sides of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally the troops or forces that you were able to identify, can you tell us generally where were they from? What was their identity?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking to Enes Taso, he told me all the units that were there, involved in the Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by Enes Taso, you're referring to Colonel Enes Taso, commander of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Commander of the tank unit, the motorised unit from Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what units Colonel Taso told you from the Yugoslav army were in the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Guards Motorised Brigade, the Novi Sad Corps, a tank unit under the command of Lieutenant Borisa Doknic from Pozarevac, and Enes Taso from Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Yugoslav forces that you were able to see at this time, were you able to tell whether the ethnic make-up of the army still reflected the ethnic make-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon your observations of the troops of the Yugoslav army troops present, did you form an opinion whether or not the command structure of those units still seemed to be functioning normally?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any reservists or reserve members of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have -- did you form an opinion regarding the functioning of their command structure? Did it appear to be functioning normally?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see members of the Territorial Defence as part of this build-up of forces in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain the composition of the members of the Territorial Defence? Were they only local people or were there people from outside the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very hard to distinguish them because for the most part they all wore civilian clothes. They were crossing the Danube en masse and coming to Vukovar and the villages around it. So it was possible only in the course of a conversation to find out who was a volunteer and who was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you form an opinion regarding whether the command structure of the Territorial Defence was functioning normally at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: These commanders of the Territorial Defence in some places, for example, in Borovo, the 1st Company, Stanko Vujanovic was a taxi driver. But in the surrounding villages, the commanders were people who were unknown to the locals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain where these unknown commanders, where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: I asked the locals who these people were. They would say discreetly that they were from Belgrade. They think that everybody comes from Belgrade. They said that they were policemen or, rather, people from the state security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us how many people you became aware were from the state security in Belgrade? How many of such people were involved with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: They led the Territorial Defence. They led these ignorant and untrained people. But how many of them there were in the villages around Vukovar, Trpinje, Sarvas. In Sarvas it was Major Cvetkovic, commander of the Territorial Defence there. In Bobota there was a policeman, and also in these other villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to July or August of 1991 and ask you whether or not you were in the vicinity of a prison and whether or not you had a conversation with a guard at that prison.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
